translations: The crowd’s voices split quickly into two groups. One side urged “shoot now,” fearing that the last day might only be a temporary lull; the other side stared at the already darkened fields, unsure where the seed would sprout after ten suns had vanished. Both sides lowered their voices, as if a louder shout would make Hou Yi release the bowstring. An old farmer lifted a handful of shriveled grain seeds, looked back and forth a few times, and finally said, “They’re afraid of fire, and they’re waiting for light.”

Hou Yi heard it, but he didn’t ask anyone for an answer. He let the arrow tip glide slowly across the sky, first pointing at the last day, then moving toward the valley below. Wherever the arrow touched was a cracked paddy, an empty well, seeds cradled by the people, and the long night that had just emerged from the heat. His arm was already trembling with fatigue, but this time he didn’t release the arrow because he was exhausted; it was because every consequence had to be weighed by him personally.

Aman lowered his head to look at his record. The first nine lines were “draw the bow, aim, release, the sun falls,” written in a clear order even if it was risky. By the tenth line, his pen hovered in midair, unsure which word to write first. Someone nearby, frantic, asked, “Historian, you should write it.” Aman, rarely stubborn, shook his head and said, “The event hasn’t happened yet, so I can’t rush it with words.” After that, he laid his pen flat on the bamboo slip, not even joking about “didn’t bring enough arrows.”

The last day seemed to feel the mountain’s silence too, and the light dimmed a layer more. People who had been curled under eaves in the distance slowly lifted their heads, no longer squinting from the sting; a fallen wheat shoot was lifted by a breeze, half a leaf unfurled, its veins still dry but no longer smoking. Hou Yi saw this tiny change and his breathing steadied. He kept the bow drawn, letting everyone know that if the sun went on its rampage, the arrow could fire at any moment; yet he didn’t let fear make the final choice for him.

But even after he laughed, he was tense, because he saw Hou Yi lift the bow again. The arrow tip aimed at the last day, and the valley was so quiet you could hear the dry grass reabsorbing moisture. Hou Yi’s arm shook, the bowstring trembled, and the people’s hearts shook along. Once that arrow left, all the scorching would end, but every dawn and dusk would be shot down together. Hou Yi saw a child by the scorched field holding half a handful of seeds; the child didn’t cry, just tucked the seeds into their chest, as if still believing that next year the light would reach them. Hou Yi slowly let the bowstring slack, didn’t fire the arrow. He drew the bow back, speaking softly but clearly to everyone: “The ninth day has fallen; the last day must stay. The world can’t be burned again, nor can it be left without light.”

When those words fell, the first to exhale was not the people, but the cracked land. A wetish hue rose along the crack’s edge, as if someone had slowly pushed the water’s veins back from the earth. The people still didn’t fully believe; someone spread their palm to test the sunlight, then flipped it over and over, as if their hand had just been redeemed from fire. Aman also tried, and immediately wrote seriously, “The last day’s temper has changed, it won’t bite for now.” After finishing, he felt the line was too solemn and wanted to delete it. Hou Yi said, “Keep it. The world should still be able to laugh.”

Hearing that, Aman was stunned. He had always thought the “Twenty Bamboo Slips of Mountains and Seas” should be written with solemnity, each word like a monk in a temple. But today he saw people crying in disaster and laughing in disaster; he saw Hou Yi’s hand tremble in pain yet still accept a casual note. He suddenly understood that humor isn’t about turning suffering into lightness, but that people in hardship are still not flattened. So he didn’t delete the line “won’t bite for now,” but added four small characters beside it: “still respectful after a laugh.”

Down below, people began to stand upright. The first to straighten was a child, his cheeks flushed from the sun, yet he held his waist like a newly sprouted sapling. Then came a woman, an old man, a youth carrying an empty basket. A man lifted a cracked wooden bucket, found it leaking at the bottom, and laughed awkwardly, “It’s suffering too.” Aman immediately replied, “A leak proves it still has a bottom line.” The crowd paused, then burst into laughter. This time the laughter wasn’t crushed by the heat; it rolled down the valley toward the fields that had not yet fully revived. The moment the last sun stayed was harder than any shot. The people first froze, then some lifted their heads to test, finding the light no longer a blade but a hand that finally understood limits. The hot wind turned into a warm breeze, the well’s mouth filled again, cracks on the ridge seeped moist earth, and a few dead grasses slowly unfurled their curled tips. An old man touched the well water, so moved he scooped a handful onto his face, then remembered the water was scarce and awkwardly stopped his hand midair. Aman wanted to laugh, but only let out a soft chuckle: “Save some energy; this one of yours costs more than all my writing.”
